chief_complaint: inversion ankle injury, pain on walking, swelling
hpi_details: 26-year-old female presents to the ED after twisting her right ankle (inversion injury) while stepping off a curb 2 hours ago. She reports immediate sharp pain, rapid swelling over the lateral malleolus, and difficulty bearing weight.
ideas: She thinks she rolled her ankle awkwardly off the curb and tore an ankle ligament or cracked a small bone.
concerns: She is worried that her ankle might be fractured and that she will be unable to walk as maid of honor at her sister's wedding next weekend.
expectations: She hopes to get an X-ray to ensure nothing is broken, a supportive walking boot or splint, and crutches to help her get around.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Lateral Ankle Sprain evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lateral Ankle Sprain is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Lateral Ankle Sprain EM: Check Ottawa Ankle Rules, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: inversion ankle injury, pain on walking, swelling

Key HPI features: A 26-year-old female presents to the clinic with inversion ankle injury, pain on walking, swelling. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Lateral Ankle Sprain EM.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lateral Ankle Sprain.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Fibular fracture without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inability to bear weight.
management_principles: Plan for Lateral Ankle Sprain EM: Check Ottawa Ankle Rules
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: inversion ankle injury, pain on walking, swelling

26-year-old female presents to the ED after twisting her right ankle (inversion injury) while stepping off a curb 2 hours ago. She reports immediate sharp pain, rapid swelling over the lateral malleolus, and difficulty bearing weight.
reference_soap.objective: Moderate swelling and ecchymosis over anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL). Tender to palpation over lateral malleolus but no bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus. Able to take 4 steps.
reference_soap.plan: Apply the Ottawa Ankle Rules before deciding on imaging; obtain ankle or foot radiographs if there is relevant bony tenderness or inability to take four steps. If fracture is excluded, use protected weight bearing, a functional brace, analgesia as appropriate, and early range-of-motion and rehabilitation exercises.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Lateral Ankle Sprain EM
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Lateral Ankle Sprain EM
Implement evidence-based management plan: Check Ottawa Ankle Rules. X-ray if indicated. RICE splint

teaching.one_liner: An inversion ankle injury causing pain and swelling, assessed with the Ottawa Ankle Rules to decide if an X-ray is needed.

must_ask.say: How did you injure your ankle?
Have you injured this ankle before?

history.answer: I twisted my right ankle when I stepped off a curb two hours ago, and now it hurts to walk and is swelling up.
The pain is only in my right ankle, right on the outer side. My left ankle and all my other joints feel completely fine.
It happened suddenly two hours ago when I misstepped off the sidewalk. The swelling started shortly after and the pain has stayed sharp.
It is a sharp, throbbing pain that is about a 6 out of 10 right now, but it spikes higher whenever I try to put weight on it.
Yes, the outside of my ankle started puffing up within thirty minutes, and there is already some mild purplish bruising.
No, I had no joint stiffness this morning. My joints felt completely normal before the injury today.
Walking, putting weight on it, or turning my foot makes the pain worse. Resting with my foot elevated helps ease the throbbing.
It hurts a lot to put weight on it, but I was able to limp and take four or five steps right after it happened to catch a cab.
I was stepping down off a curb onto the road, lost my footing on the edge, and my right foot rolled inward underneath me.
I felt a sudden sharp pull and stretching sensation, but I did not hear or feel a loud pop or snapping sound.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweating.
No, I have never sprained, twisted, or broken this ankle or any other joint before.
No, I have not had any unusual fatigue, low-grade fevers, or weight loss.
No, I do not have any skin rashes, mouth sores, hair loss, or red and irritated eyes.
No, I have never had morning lower back stiffness, pain in my heels, or swollen sausage-like fingers or toes.
No, I have not had any diarrhea, burning when urinating, unusual discharge, or sore throats in recent weeks.
No, I do not take water pills, and I haven't eaten large feasts of seafood or red meat, nor engaged in binge drinking.
No, I have never had steroid injections, surgery on my joints, or artificial joint implants.
I have been with my partner in a monogamous relationship for two years, and I have no history or symptoms of sexually transmitted infections.
I think I rolled my foot really badly when stepping off the curb and either badly sprained it or broke a bone.
I'm worried it might be fractured and I won't be able to walk down the aisle as maid of honor at my sister's wedding next Saturday.
I'm hoping to get an X-ray to check for any broken bones, and maybe a supportive brace and crutches so I can move around.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or arthritis.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I only drink socially on occasion, perhaps a glass of wine or beer once or twice a month.
I work as an office administrator at a desk job, and I live in an apartment building with an elevator.
No one in my family has rheumatoid arthritis, gout, ankylosing spondylitis, or other chronic joint conditions.
My last period was two weeks ago and my cycle is regular every twenty-eight days. There is no chance of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable while seated, in mild distress when attempting to move or place weight on the right foot, with no signs of systemic illness.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7°C, SpO2 99% on room air.

Moderate swelling and ecchymosis over the right anterior talofibular ligament; tenderness to palpation over the lateral ligaments, but no bony tenderness along the posterior edge or distal 6 cm of the lateral or medial malleolus, base of the fifth metatarsal, or navicular bone; active inversion and plantarflexion provoke pain.
Antalgic gait favoring the right leg, but able to bear weight and take four consecutive steps unassisted.
No tophi, psoriasis plaques, malar rash, or nail changes; ecchymosis and soft tissue swelling are strictly confined to the right lateral ankle.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally, and capillary refill is under 2 seconds across all toes.
Intact sensation to light touch across the superficial peroneal, deep peroneal, sural, saphenous, and tibial nerve distributions bilaterally.
